thread.title: The Big Picture: The Race -- No, the Sprint -- to Fair Value

title: The Big Picture: The Race -- No, the Sprint -- to Fair Value
text:
HOME > Our View > The Big Picture > The Race -- No, the Sprint --... The Big Picture Archive Last Update: 18-Jan-19 15:40 ET The Race -- No, the Sprint -- to Fair Value
Economic growth is slowing and earnings growth is, too. Given that, how much would you pay for every dollar of earnings?
It's an important question for any investor. The answer in early 2019 is that investors will pay more today than they would in December 2018, because the economic and earnings growth outlook today is not as dark as it was made out to be in December.
There are some reasons for that, which we will address today.
For now, consider this: a market trading at 14.2x forward twelve-month earnings when we provided our market view update on December 21 is now trading at 15.6x forward twelve-month earnings.
The multiple expansion, just like last year's multiple compression, has been price-driven as investors have been running -- nay, sprinting -- back into the stock market.
The Race Is On
As of this writing, the S&P 500 is up 6.5% year-to-date. That's a big move alright, but it isn't the biggest.
The Russell 2000 is up 9.8%; the S&P Midcap 400 Index is up 9.2%; and the Nasdaq Composite is up 8.1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, up 5.7%, is bringing up the rear in a very fast field.
They could all take a V-shaped victory lap, but alas, the race isn't over. There is a long way to go still, as everyone discovered in 2018, making this race a marathon and not a sprint.
Be that as it may, it has been a very fast start catalyzed by the following factors: The Christmas Eve washout that saw the S&P 500 drop 65 points, or 2.7%, to 2351.10 -- a 20% decline from the September all-time high and a 14.8% decline in December alone That move engendered a belief that the market had gotten deeply oversold and was primed for a rebound effort. The release of the stronger than expected December employment report That report made it evident to market participants that the U.S. economy, supported by healthy hiring activity and rising wage growth, was not at risk of an imminent recession. The acknowledgment from Fed Chair Powell (on the same day as the employment report) that the Fed will be closely watching market signals and will be patient with its monetary policy approach. Mr. Powell also added that the Fed would alter its balance sheet normalization effort if necessary. That acknowledgment was music to the ears of a market that had feared the Fed being too aggressive with its policy and killing the economic expansion. In market parlance, Mr. Powell's acknowledgment that day was the born-again moment for the "Fed put" that has been a lifeline for the stock market since 2009. Constructive headlines on trade negotiations with China Deputy trade officials met in Beijing in the second week of January. They didn't strike a deal, nor were they expected to, but a two-day meeting that was extended to a third day fostered a sense of hope that progress on a trade deal was being made. Recent reports have also intimated that U.S. and Chinese officials are floating proposals that could serve as a framework for getting a comprehensive deal done before the March 2 deadline. The resilience to selling efforts The S&P 500 has risen as much as 13.8% from its Dec. 24 low and is overbought on a short-term basis. Still, it has not relented to selling interest, even in the face of negative news catalysts. That resilience has led to a gains that has led, well, to further gains.
Running Uphill
The stock market isn't going to be able to keep running at its current pace. It's simply too fast for an uphill course that has a high degree of difficulty. Economic and earnings growth is slowing . Both might remain positive this year, yet neither is expected to be as strong as last year when the S&P 500 traded between 16x and 18.7x forward twelve-month earnings for the first three quarters. While there is a hopeful tone surrounding trade negotiations with China, nothing can be taken for granted considering China has yet to float a concession that it will acquiesce to U.S. demands regarding forced technology transfers and intellectual property rights. The partisan standoff over funding for border security, which has led to the partial government shutdown, is laying some worrisome groundwork in front of the need later this year to raise the debt ceiling. A fiscal Q1 revenue warning from Apple (AAPL) and an FY19 earnings warning from FedEx (FDX) are high-profile reminders that the risk to earnings estimates is skewed to the downside in 2019, not to the upside. China, Europe, and Japan are all experiencing an economic slowdown, which doesn't make for the best selling environment. Corporate debt, as a percentage of GDP, is at an all-time high, which will be problematic if/when interest rates rise and/or demand slows. The Federal Reserve could change its tune if the stock market keeps rallying and economic data lives up to the Fed's higher expectations, meaning the stock market could find itself right back in the same place of fearing a hawkish-minded Fed.
What It All Means
Our aim isn't to get caught up in everything that could go wrong, only to point out that the political, economic, and earnings environment out there isn't as sanguine as the January rally would lead one to think it is.
To be fair, things aren't as bad as feared in December either. That's really the crux of the trading matter right now.
The stock market was pricing in a recession in December and now it is pricing out a recession. It was pricing in a hawkish Fed in December and now it is pricing in a more dovish-minded Fed.
The stock market, therefore, is getting back to a middle ground that has it trading above its 10-year average P/E ratio (14.6) but below its 5-year average P/E ratio (16.4), per FactSet data.
That looks to be an appropriate place for now as some of the known unknowns, like Brexit, the government shutdown, and the trade negotiations with China, continue to hang in the balance along with earnings estimate revisions.
This market has the same feel as the market did in January 2018 . The two periods, however, are not alike.
In January 2018, the market was rallying on the enthusiasm for the fiscal stimulus package and an expectation that both economic and earnings growth would be accelerating in 2018.
Today, the market is rallying on the relief that things aren't as bad as feared while recognizing that economic and earnings growth will be decelerating in 2019. There has been some multiple expansion on the former, but largely because the multiple compression in December 2018 was overdone.
Further multiple expansion should be harder to come by, absent an actual trade agreement with China that ignites some animal spirits, because there will be a higher degree of difficulty in 2019 for generating every dollar of earnings.
The stock market has sprinted out of the gate in 2019 to a fair value, yet this marathon is just getting started.
